title: Superpolynomial Extended Frege lower bounds
formal: Is classical Extended Frege not polynomially bounded? Precisely, for every pair of integers \(C\ge1,c\ge1\), does there exist a propositional tautology \(\varphi\) such that every Extended Frege proof \(\pi\) of \(\varphi\) has binary encoding length \(|\pi|>C(|\varphi|+2)^c\)? The formula and proof encodings and the fixed proof rules are specified below.
definitions:
A propositional formula is a finite syntax tree built from variables \(v_i\), indexed by \(i\in\mathbb N\), unary negation and binary material implication. Its Boolean value under an assignment \(v_i\mapsto\{0,1\}\) is defined recursively, with \(A	o B\) false exactly when A is true and B is false. A tautology is true under every assignment to its variables. Let code(a), for \(a\ge0\), be \(1^b0\) followed by the b-bit binary expansion of a+1, with \(b=\lfloor\log_2(a+1)floor+1\). Encode \(v_i\) as 00 followed by code(i), \(
eg A\) as 01 followed by the encoding of A, and \(A	o B\) as 10 followed by the encodings of A and B. This prefix syntax contains the whole formula tree, not a circuit or a program generating it; \(|\varphi|\) is its bit length. Fix the three classical Frege axiom schemes \(A	o(B	o A)\), \((A	o(B	o C))	o((A	o B)	o(A	o C))\), and \((
eg B	o
eg A)	o(A	o B)\). An instance substitutes arbitrary formulas for A, B and C consistently. Modus ponens infers B from two earlier lines A and \(A	o B\). An extension introduction adds two consecutive lines \(e	o	heta\) and \(	heta	o e\), where e is a variable absent from the target formula, theta and every line before this pair. The defining formula theta may use variables of the target and previously introduced extension variables, so definitions are acyclic. Freshness is checked before the pair, not between its two lines. There are no unproved hypotheses. A proof is a finite nonempty list of lines justified by these axiom schemes, modus ponens or such an extension pair; its last line is exactly the target formula and contains no extension variables. Earlier lines can be cited any number of times. There is no depth bound, tree-like proof restriction or restriction on the sizes of intermediate formulas. For a complete proof encoding, first write code(m) for its number of lines, and then encode each line with a two-bit tag, its metadata and its entire formula in the prefix syntax above. Tag 00 stores the axiom-scheme number 1, 2 or 3 with code; tag 01 stores with code the two earlier, one-based line indices for modus ponens, in the order A then A implies B; tag 10 stores with code the index of the fresh extension variable and must be followed immediately by a tag-11 line giving the reverse implication for the same definition. Tag 11 has no metadata and is valid only as that second line of an extension pair. The first extension formula uniquely determines theta, and both implication formulas are fully written and counted. Missing or trailing bits and invalid justifications are rejected. The proof length counts all bits, including the line count, formulas, variable indices, rule tags and inference references. This is a fixed polynomial-time checkable presentation of classical EF, polynomially equivalent to the usual finite Frege bases with extension. EF is complete, so every tautology has some finite proof; the issue is a common polynomial bound. The chosen binary encoding and paired extension rule fix presentation details without changing polynomial boundedness. The hard formula may depend on C and c; no polynomial-time procedure generating a hard family is imposed.
answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked proof of the displayed lower-bound assertion or its logical negation. The affirmative answer must, for every polynomial bound \(C(n+2)^c\), establish a tautology whose every valid EF proof exceeds that bound. The negative answer must establish fixed integers C,c for which every tautology has some valid EF proof of length at most \(C(|\varphi|+2)^c\); it need not give a polynomial-time proof-search algorithm. A bound for one search procedure, for bounded-depth or ordinary Frege, for a different logic, or for an algebraic encoding without a valid polynomial-size propositional translation does not settle this target.
why: Extended Frege captures a powerful form of efficient propositional reasoning with reusable definitions. A superpolynomial lower bound would cross one of the central barriers in proof complexity and clarify whether a standard, highly expressive certificate language necessarily fails on some short true statements.

importance.reason: A defining open lower-bound problem for strong propositional reasoning, closely connected to bounded arithmetic, circuit complexity, and the limits of efficiently checkable certificates.

progress.text: Cook and Reckhow define propositional proof-system efficiency and formalize the extension rule. Their equivalence theorems make EF polynomial boundedness independent of standard presentations; Cook’s posted correction to Corollary 4.7 keeps the coNP-versus-NP premise explicit.

Wigderson’s book lists superpolynomial unrestricted Frege lower bounds as open and distinguishes the additional sharing available in Extended Frege. Lower bounds for the weaker system would not automatically apply to EF.

Pich and Santhanam give implications from EF lower bounds to \(\mathrm P\ne\mathrm{NP}\) with additional formal provability hypotheses. The checked preprint does not give an unconditional EF lower bound.

Hsieh, Jain, Li and Mathialagan construct succinct non-interactive arguments for NP under promise derandomization, LWE, SXDH and a bounded-arithmetic hardness-certification assumption. The formal unprovability premise differs from the unconditional proof-size target.

Alekseev’s journal paper proves an exponential bit-size lower bound for algebraic Binary Value Principle refutations and explicitly explains why it does not give a Frege or EF lower bound for propositional tautologies.

Akbar Tabatabai reports exponential separations between EF systems for intuitionistic substructural and linear logics. The preprint’s stated scope differs from this classical system; its proof was not independently verified.

status_note: The June 2026 algebraic paper explicitly distinguishes its theorem from the unresolved classical EF problem, and the checked cryptographic paper likewise treats EF hardness as an unresolved issue. The August 2026 preprint concerns different logics. A bounded primary-source search on 14 September 2026 found no verified classical EF resolution. The checked Pich–Santhanam version is the 2023 preprint, not its inaccessible journal version; the cited proofs have not been independently recertified.

context_blocks.text: Extension variables let a proof name a formula once and reuse its name. This can represent shared computations economically, as a Boolean circuit shares intermediate gates. Expanding all abbreviations into formula trees can cause an exponential increase in length, so a lower bound that counts only ordinary Frege proofs does not automatically survive the extension rule.

The question concerns the existence of short certificates, not the time required to discover them. A particular proof search method might take exponential time even though another method could find a short proof; conversely, a proof-size lower bound would constrain every method that outputs an EF derivation. The input length is the final tautology’s actual encoding length, so a lower bound exponential in a smaller hidden parameter may still be only polynomial in the input.

If \(\mathrm{NP}\ne \mathrm{coNP}\), every polynomial-time verifiable propositional proof system has hard tautologies, including EF. The converse for this particular system is unknown: showing that EF is inefficient does not rule out a different proof system that gives short certificates for all tautologies. This is why an EF lower bound would be a major advance without automatically constituting a proof of \(\mathrm{NP}\ne \mathrm{coNP}\). Cook’s author page corrects the premise of Corollary 4.7 in the original paper to coNP differing from NP; a P-versus-NP separation alone is not the stated premise.

Recent algebraic lower bounds illustrate an encoding issue. Alekseev proves exponential bit-size lower bounds for an extension of polynomial calculus that can simulate EF on suitable propositional translations. The hard Binary Value Principle instance is not the corresponding translation of a polynomial-size CNF. The paper explicitly explains that its result therefore does not yield a Frege or EF lower bound.

Pich and Santhanam give implications from EF lower bounds to \(\mathrm{P}\ne \mathrm{NP}\) under additional bounded-arithmetic assumptions. This explores the consequences of proof-complexity hypotheses without proving an unconditional EF lower bound.

Hsieh and coauthors construct succinct arguments under derandomization, cryptographic, and formal unprovability assumptions. Their result connects the difficulty of certifying hard tautologies to cryptography; it does not establish the unconditional size lower bound asked for here.

The use of classical implication matters. Recent lower bounds for Extended Frege systems of intuitionistic or linear logics concern different rules and valid formulas. The August 2026 preprint on those systems therefore cannot be read as a solution of the unrestricted classical problem fixed here.

sentences: Extended Frege is a classical propositional proof system that can introduce reusable names for previously specified formulas.
The question asks whether no single polynomial bounds the shortest proof of every tautology by its statement length.
The target counts the full encoded proof and allows arbitrary depth and reuse of earlier lines.
Its negation would give short proofs for every tautology without necessarily making them easy to find.
Recent conditional, algebraic and intuitionistic results do not supply the unrestricted classical lower bound.
